title: Isaiah 44:9–20
context: After 44:1–8—Fear not, O Jacob my servant, Jeshurun chosen; water on the thirsty and Spirit on offspring; I am the first and I am the last; besides me there is no god; you are my witnesses; there is no Rock—the word turns: All who fashion idols are nothing, and the things they delight in do not profit. Their witnesses neither see nor know. Craftsmen are only human; the same tree is fuel, bread, and a god; they pray Deliver me to a block of wood; a deluded heart cannot say, Is there not a lie in my right hand?

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Historic words on fashioners of idols who are nothing, craftsmen who are only human, the ironsmith faint over coals, the carpenter shaping a man to dwell in a house, one tree for fire and for a god, Deliver me to a block of wood, eyes shut so they cannot see, and a lie in the right hand—so each camp speaks in its own voice beside Isaiah 44:9–20.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Delectable things—Their idols, in which they take so much pleasure. They—They that make them, are witnesses against themselves, and against their idols, because they know they are the work of their own hands. See not—Have neither sense nor understanding, therefore they have just cause to be ashamed of their folly, in worshipping such senseless things. Men—They are of mankind, and therefore cannot possibly make a god. Fallen down—he makes his fire and his god of the same materials, distinguished only by the art of man. For he—God. Not as if God did make men wicked; he only permits them so to be, and orders, and over-rules their wickedness to his own glorious ends. Ashes—An unprofitable and pernicious food, and no less unsatisfying and mischievous is the worship of idols. Is there not—What is this idol which I set at my right-hand? Is it not a lie, which tho’ it pretends to be a god, yet, in truth is nothing but vanity and falsehood?
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Isa 44:9–20)

reformed.quote: Formers of a graven image are vanity; desirable things do not profit; worshippers themselves are witnesses that the idols neither see nor know; conscience is a witness how vain. Who is the maker of God? Madness to frame gods; as soon as stone or wood is polished they ascribe divinity. Same wood: fuel, bread, then a god. Residue made a god: Deliver me, for thou art my god. They have not known—God hath blinded them by a righteous judgment (Rom 1:28); takes away the light of his Spirit; yet blame lies with men who deserve it and voluntarily shut their eyes. He feedeth on ashes: empty, puffed up with deceptions. Is there not a lie in my right hand: examine actions; try everything by the standard God laid down.

verses.text: All who fashion idols are nothing, and the things they delight in do not profit. Their witnesses neither see nor know, that they may be put to shame.
verses.arminianNotes:
All who fashion idols are nothing, and the things they delight in do not profit. Their witnesses neither see nor know, that they may be put to shame. Wesley: Delectable things—Their idols, in which they take so much pleasure. They—They that make them, are witnesses against themselves, and against their idols, because they know they are the work of their own hands. See not—Have neither sense nor understanding, therefore they have just cause to be ashamed of their folly, in worshipping such senseless things.

Arminian hearing: idols are delectable things that do not profit; makers are witnesses against themselves; the images neither see nor know. Shared: fashioners are nothing; witnesses neither see nor know; shame. Historic ANE idol-makers, not the Christ-Servant of 42:1–9, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Wesley’s “Delectable things” is his lemma for “the things they delight in,” not a different verse. Prefer no keyContrast: 9 is shared satire. Match v. 8: the LORD’s witnesses see and know; these neither see nor know. Match v. 10: who fashions a god that profits nothing.
verses.reformedNotes:
Formers of a graven image are vanity. Calvin: desirable things (idols and their worship) do not profit; worshippers themselves are witnesses that the idols neither see nor know; conscience is a witness how vain; they shall be ashamed.

Reformed hearing: formers are vanity; conscience itself witnesses the vanity; shame follows. Shared with Wesley: idols do not profit; makers are witnesses; they neither see nor know; shame. Historic Babylon-era craftsmen, not a newspaper, not a living politician. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s “Formers of a graven image are vanity” is his lemma for “All who fashion idols are nothing”; “desirable things” for “the things they delight in.” Prefer no keyContrast: 9 is shared satire. Match v. 8: no Rock besides; these witnesses cannot see. Match v. 10: who is the maker of God?

verses.text: Who fashions a god or casts an idol that is profitable for nothing?
verses.arminianNotes:
Who fashions a god or casts an idol that is profitable for nothing? Wesley has no extra lemma. Paraphrase from v. 9 and v. 11 honestly: delectable things do not profit; they that make them know they are the work of their own hands; men are of mankind and therefore cannot possibly make a god. Do not invent unique Wesley sentences here.

Arminian hearing: no craftsman can fashion a profitable god; the work of their own hands cannot be God. Shared: who fashions a god; profitable for nothing. Historic idol-casters, not a newspaper. Prefer no keyContrast: 10 is shared satire. Match v. 9: nothing and no profit. Match v. 11: craftsmen are only human.
verses.reformedNotes:
Who is the maker of God? Calvin: madness to frame gods; as soon as stone or wood is polished they ascribe divinity. All images by which God is represented are vain and useless; nothing can be learned from them but falsehood.

Reformed hearing: madness to frame a god; polished wood is not divinity; images teach falsehood. Shared with Wesley: who fashions a god; profitable for nothing; men cannot make a god. Historic ANE image-makers, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s “Who is the maker of God?” is his lemma for “Who fashions a god.” Prefer no keyContrast: 10 is shared satire. Match v. 9: vanity. Match v. 11: craftsmen are of men.

verses.text: Behold, all his companions shall be put to shame, and the craftsmen are only human. Let them all assemble, let them stand forth. They shall be terrified; they shall be put to shame together.
verses.arminianNotes:
Behold, all his companions shall be put to shame, and the craftsmen are only human. Let them all assemble, let them stand forth. They shall be terrified; they shall be put to shame together. Wesley: Men—They are of mankind, and therefore cannot possibly make a god. Together—Tho’ all combine together, they shall be filled with fear and confusion, when God shall plead his cause against them.

Arminian hearing: craftsmen are mankind, so they cannot make a god; even combined they meet fear and confusion when God pleads his cause. Shared: companions ashamed; craftsmen only human; they assemble and are put to shame together. Historic craftsmen, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Wesley’s “Men” is his lemma for “the craftsmen are only human”; “Together” for “put to shame together”; “Tho’” is his spelling. Prefer no keyContrast: 11 is shared satire. Match v. 10: who fashions a god. Match v. 12: the ironsmith at the coals is that same man.
verses.reformedNotes:
All companions ashamed; craftsmen are of men. Calvin: though they all assemble they shall fear and be ashamed together. Conscience sometimes constrains them to tremble.

Reformed hearing: companions ashamed; craftsmen of men; assembly ends in fear; conscience makes them tremble. Shared with Wesley: craftsmen are men; they combine and are ashamed together. Historic ANE craftsmen, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s “craftsmen are of men” is his lemma for “the craftsmen are only human.” Prefer no keyContrast: 11 is shared satire. Match v. 10: maker of God is madness. Match v. 12: the hungry ironsmith is that man.

verses.text: The ironsmith takes a cutting tool and works it over the coals. He fashions it with hammers and works it with his strong arm. He becomes hungry, and his strength fails; he drinks no water and is faint.
verses.arminianNotes:
The ironsmith takes a cutting tool and works it over the coals. He fashions it with hammers and works it with his strong arm. He becomes hungry, and his strength fails; he drinks no water and is faint. Wesley: Faint—This is mentioned as an evidence of great zeal and industry in carrying on this work; so that they forget or neglect to eat and drink.

Arminian hearing: hunger and faintness prove zeal; they forget to eat and drink over the coals. Shared: ironsmith, coals, hammers, strong arm, hungry and faint. Historic ANE ironsmith, not a newspaper, not a living politician. Prefer no keyContrast: 12 is shared satire. Match v. 11: craftsmen are only human—he grows hungry. Match v. 13: the carpenter stretches a line with the same human craft.
verses.reformedNotes:
Long description of tools to shake stupidity. Calvin: Hungry, drinks no water: evidence of zeal; they burn with ardor; lust like a gad-fly. Calvin later illustrates inordinate zeal by Papists and Turks—his illustration, not the verse’s historic referent; the verse itself is ANE craftsmen at the coals.

Reformed hearing: tools listed to shake stupidity; hunger is zeal; ardor burns; lust like a gad-fly. Shared with Wesley: faintness as evidence of zeal; they neglect eat and drink. Historic Babylon-era ironsmith, not a newspaper, not a living politician. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s Papists/Turks are later illustrations of inordinate zeal, not the historic craftsmen of this verse. Prefer no keyContrast: 12 is shared satire. Match v. 11: only human. Match v. 13: carpenter’s line is the same human work.

verses.text: The carpenter stretches a line; he marks it out with a pencil. He shapes it with planes and marks it with a compass. He shapes it into the figure of a man, with the beauty of a man, to dwell in a house.
verses.arminianNotes:
The carpenter stretches a line; he marks it out with a pencil. He shapes it with planes and marks it with a compass. He shapes it into the figure of a man, with the beauty of a man, to dwell in a house. Wesley: According to—In the same comely shape and proportions which are in a living man. House—In the dwelling-house of him that made it.

Arminian hearing: the figure copies a living man’s proportions; it dwells in the maker’s house. Shared: carpenter, line, pencil, planes, compass; figure of a man to dwell in a house. Historic ANE carpenter, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Wesley’s “According to” is his lemma for “the beauty of a man”; “House” for “to dwell in a house.” Prefer no keyContrast: 13 is shared satire. Match v. 12: ironsmith’s arm; here the carpenter’s line. Match v. 14: the timber is cut for this figure.
verses.reformedNotes:
Figure of a man to abide in the house. Calvin: idle, without motion.

Reformed hearing: the man-figure abides in a house, idle, without motion. Shared with Wesley: shaped as a man; dwells in a house. Historic carpenter’s idol, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s “abide in the house” is his lemma for “to dwell in a house”; “idle, without motion” is his comment, not a different English Bible. Prefer no keyContrast: 13 is shared satire. Match v. 12: tools and hunger. Match v. 14–15: the tree that will be this idle figure is also fuel.

verses.text: He cuts down cedars, or he chooses a cypress tree or an oak and lets it grow strong among the trees of the forest. He plants a cedar and the rain nourishes it.
verses.arminianNotes:
He cuts down cedars, or he chooses a cypress tree or an oak and lets it grow strong among the trees of the forest. He plants a cedar and the rain nourishes it. Wesley: Oak—Which afford the best and most durable timber. Strengtheneth—He plants, and with care and diligence improves those trees, that he or his posterity may thence have materials for their images, and those things which belong to them.

Arminian hearing: oak is durable timber; he plants and improves so he or his posterity may have materials for images. Shared: cedars, cypress, oak; planted and rain-nourished. Historic forest timber for ANE images, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Wesley’s “Oak” and “Strengtheneth” are his lemmas for choosing an oak that grows strong and planting a cedar. Prefer no keyContrast: 14 is shared satire. Match v. 13: timber for the figure of a man. Match v. 15: then it becomes fuel.
verses.reformedNotes:
They plant and wait for timber. Calvin: rebellion and obstinacy, not a sudden impulse. Seed of this madness in us unless cleansed by the Spirit.

Reformed hearing: planting and waiting is obstinacy, not a sudden impulse; the seed of this madness is in us unless the Spirit cleanses. Shared with Wesley: they plant and improve trees for images. Historic forest and rain, not a newspaper. No millennial fight. Prefer no keyContrast: Calvin’s Spirit-cleansing of the seed is not a fight with Wesley’s durable oak; 14 is shared satire. Match v. 13: the figure waits on this timber. Match v. 15: same wood becomes fire and a god. Do not invent open theism: the planter is obstinate; God is not learning from the forest.

verses.text: Then it becomes fuel for a man. He takes a part of it and warms himself; he kindles a fire and bakes bread. Also he makes a god and worships it; he makes it an idol and falls down before it.
verses.arminianNotes:
Then it becomes fuel for a man. He takes a part of it and warms himself; he kindles a fire and bakes bread. Also he makes a god and worships it; he makes it an idol and falls down before it. Wesley: Fallen down—Having related the practices of idolaters, he now discovers the folly of them, that he makes his fire and his god of the same materials, distinguished only by the art of man.

Arminian hearing: fire and god from the same materials; only man’s art distinguishes them; falling down is the folly. Shared loudly: same wood warms, bakes bread, and is worshiped. Historic stock of a tree, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Wesley’s “Fallen down” is his lemma for “falls down before it.” Prefer no keyContrast: 15 is shared satire. Match v. 14: the planted cedar is this fuel. Match v. 16–17: half burned, residue made a god.
verses.reformedNotes:
Same wood: fuel, bread, then a god. Calvin: stupidity if they do not consider how bountifully God provided the tree. Horace’s jest (fig-tree/Priapus) may be mentioned as Calvin’s citation, not as the verse’s historic referent.

Reformed hearing: one tree is fire, bread, and a god; they do not consider God’s bounty in the tree. Shared with Wesley: fire and god from the same materials. Historic ANE wood, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Horace’s fig-tree/Priapus is Calvin’s citation, not Isaiah’s historic referent; the verse is Babylon-era craftsmen and a stock of wood. Prefer no keyContrast: 15 is shared satire. Match v. 14: rain-nourished timber. Match v. 16–17: Aha, I am warm; Deliver me.

verses.text: Half of it he burns in the fire. Over the half he eats meat; he roasts it and is satisfied. Also he warms himself and says, “Aha, I am warm, I have seen the fire!”
verses.arminianNotes:
Half of it he burns in the fire. Over the half he eats meat; he roasts it and is satisfied. Also he warms himself and says, Aha, I am warm, I have seen the fire! Wesley has no extra lemma on this verse. Quote-honesty: Wesley’s “Seen—I have felt the warmth of it” is his lemma for “I have seen the fire,” though some printings sit it under 17; it belongs here. Paraphrase from v. 15 honestly: he makes his fire and his god of the same materials. Do not invent unique Wesley sentences.

Arminian hearing: half burned; he eats and is satisfied; Aha, I am warm—he has felt the fire. Shared: half in the fire; roast and warm; Aha. Historic same tree, not a newspaper. Prefer no keyContrast: 16 is shared satire. Match v. 15: fuel and bread. Match v. 17: the rest becomes his god.
verses.reformedNotes:
Aha I am warm. Calvin: same wood—fuel, bread, then a god. Stupidity if they do not consider how bountifully God provided the tree.

Reformed hearing: Aha, I am warm, names the same wood that will be prayed to. Shared with Wesley: half burned; he eats and warms; the fire is felt. Historic ANE fire and meat, not a newspaper. Prefer no keyContrast: 16 is shared satire. Match v. 15: fuel and bread. Match v. 17: residue made a god, Deliver me.

verses.text: And the rest of it he makes into a god, his idol, and falls down to it and worships it. He prays to it and says, “Deliver me, for you are my god!”
verses.arminianNotes:
And the rest of it he makes into a god, his idol, and falls down to it and worships it. He prays to it and says, Deliver me, for you are my god! Wesley: He eateth—He dresses flesh for his eating. Thin; do not invent unique Wesley sentences. Quote-honesty: “He eateth” is Wesley’s lemma for dressing flesh, nearer v. 16’s roast; he has no extra lemma on the residue made a god. Paraphrase from v. 15 honestly: fire and god of the same materials, distinguished only by the art of man; he falls down.

Arminian hearing: the rest is made a god; he prays Deliver me to what his hands leftover. Shared loudly: residue is a god; falls down; Deliver me, for you are my god. Historic block of wood, not a newspaper, not a living politician. Prefer no keyContrast: 17 is shared satire. Match v. 16: half burned, rest leftover. Match v. 15: falls down before it. Match v. 19–20: abomination; lie in the right hand.
verses.reformedNotes:
Residue made a god: Deliver me, for thou art my god. Calvin: same wood as the fire. Stupidity if they do not consider how bountifully God provided the tree.

Reformed hearing: leftover wood is prayed to as god; Deliver me names the folly. Shared with Wesley: rest made a god; falls down; Deliver me. Historic ANE idol from the same tree, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s “thou art my god” is his lemma for “you are my god.” Prefer no keyContrast: 17 is shared satire. Match v. 16: Aha, I am warm. Match v. 18: they know not.

verses.text: They know not, nor do they discern, for he has shut their eyes, so that they cannot see, and their hearts, so that they cannot understand.
verses.arminianNotes:
They know not, nor do they discern, for he has shut their eyes, so that they cannot see, and their hearts, so that they cannot understand. Wesley: Not known—This shews that they have not the understanding of a man. For he—God. Not as if God did make men wicked; he only permits them so to be, and orders, and over-rules their wickedness to his own glorious ends.

Arminian hearing: they lack a man’s understanding; “for he” is God, who does not make men wicked but permits them so to be, and orders and over-rules their wickedness to his own glorious ends. Shared: they know not; eyes shut; hearts cannot understand. Historic idolaters of this satire, not a newspaper, not Judah-as-blind-servant of 42:18–25 except as the same book’s larger polemic. Quote-honesty: Wesley’s “Not known” is his lemma for “They know not”; “For he—God” is his reading of “he has shut their eyes”; “shews” is his spelling. No open theism: he permits and over-rules; he is not learning from events. Match v. 17: Deliver me to leftover wood. Match v. 19: no one considers.
verses.reformedNotes:
They have not known or understood. Calvin: impossible they fell into this if any spark of reason remained; they have degenerated into beasts. For he hath smeared their eyes. Calvin prefers: God hath blinded them by a righteous judgment (Rom 1:28 reprobate mind); takes away the light of his Spirit; arms Satan with the efficiency of error (2 Thess 2:11). Yet blame lies with men who deserve it and voluntarily shut their eyes. Do not throw on God the blame of this blindness.

Reformed hearing: no spark of reason left; God smears/shuts their eyes as judicial hardening; reprobate mind (Rom 1:28); 2 Thess 2:11; yet they voluntarily shut their eyes, so blame is theirs. Shared with Wesley: they know not; eyes shut; hearts cannot understand. Historic idolaters, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s “smeared their eyes” is his lemma for “he has shut their eyes.” No open theism: he judicially blinds; he is not discovering whom to harden. Match v. 17: Deliver me. Match v. 19: it does not return into their heart.
verses.keyContrast: Arminian readings, with Wesley, take “for he” as God, yet not as if God did make men wicked: he only permits them so to be, and orders and over-rules their wickedness to his own glorious ends. Reformed readings, with Calvin, take the shutting of eyes as righteous judgment: God hath smeared/shut their eyes, given them up to a reprobate mind (Rom 1:28), taken away the light of his Spirit, and armed Satan with the efficiency of error (2 Thess 2:11)—yet the blame is theirs because they deserve it and voluntarily shut their eyes; do not throw on God the blame of this blindness. Shared: they know not nor discern; eyes shut; hearts cannot understand. Historic idol-satire, not a millennial camp fight, not a newspaper. Do not invent open theism: Wesley’s God permits and overrules; he is not learning from events. Calvin’s God judicially blinds; he is not discovering whom to harden.

verses.text: No one considers, nor is there knowledge or discernment to say, “Half of it I burned in the fire; I also baked bread on its coals; I roasted meat and have eaten. And shall I make the rest of it an abomination? Shall I fall down before a block of wood?”
verses.arminianNotes:
No one considers, nor is there knowledge or discernment to say, Half of it I burned in the fire; I also baked bread on its coals; I roasted meat and have eaten. And shall I make the rest of it an abomination? Shall I fall down before a block of wood? Wesley has no extra lemma. Paraphrase from v. 18 and v. 20 honestly: they have not the understanding of a man; a deceived heart has turned from the way of truth; he cannot say, Is there not a lie in my right hand? So here: no one considers to say, shall I fall down before a block of wood? Do not invent unique Wesley sentences.

Arminian hearing: no consideration; half burned, bread baked, rest an abomination if he fell down to a block of wood. Shared loudly: same wood is fire, bread, meat, and an abomination; a block of wood. Historic stock of a tree, not a newspaper. Prefer no keyContrast: 19 is shared satire, not the permission-versus-hardening fork of v. 18. Match v. 15–17: fire, bread, Deliver me. Match v. 18: they cannot understand. Match v. 20: lie in the right hand.
verses.reformedNotes:
It doth not return into their heart. Calvin: they refuse to consider; sloth without excuse; they wish to be deceived; this vice is rebellion not mere first corruption.

Reformed hearing: it does not return into the heart; they refuse to consider; they wish to be deceived; rebellion, not mere first corruption. Shared with Wesley: no one considers; half burned; shall I fall down before a block of wood? Historic ANE wood, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s “It doth not return into their heart” is his lemma for “No one considers.” Prefer no keyContrast: 19 is shared satire, not the permission-versus-hardening fork of v. 18. Match v. 18: eyes shut. Match v. 20: feedeth on ashes; a lie in the right hand.

verses.text: He feeds on ashes; a deluded heart has led him astray, and he cannot deliver himself or say, “Is there not a lie in my right hand?”
verses.arminianNotes:
He feeds on ashes; a deluded heart has led him astray, and he cannot deliver himself or say, Is there not a lie in my right hand? Wesley: Ashes—An unprofitable and pernicious food, and no less unsatisfying and mischievous is the worship of idols. Deceived heart—A mind corrupted and deceived by deep prejudice, gross error, and especially by his own lusts. Turned—From the way of truth. Deliver—From the snares and dangers of idolatry. Is there not—What is this idol which I set at my right-hand, as the true God is said in scripture to be at the right-hand of his people; which I highly honour, for the most honourable place was on the right-hand; to which I look for relief and assistance? What, I say, is this idol? Is it not a lie, which tho’ it pretends to be a god, yet, in truth is nothing but vanity and falsehood?

Arminian hearing: ashes are pernicious food; idol-worship is the same; the heart is corrupted by prejudice, error, and lusts; turned from truth; he cannot deliver himself from idolatry’s snares; the right-hand idol is a lie, vanity and falsehood. Shared loudly: feeds on ashes; deluded heart; cannot deliver himself; lie in the right hand. Historic right-hand idol, not a newspaper, not a living politician. Quote-honesty: Wesley’s “Deceived heart” and “Turned” are his lemmas for “a deluded heart has led him astray”; “Deliver” for “he cannot deliver himself”; “tho’” is his spelling. Prefer no keyContrast: 20 is shared satire—the permission-versus-hardening fork stays on v. 18. Match v. 17: Deliver me to leftover wood—he cannot deliver himself. Match v. 19: block of wood. Match v. 8: no Rock besides; this right hand holds a lie.
verses.reformedNotes:
He feedeth on ashes. Calvin: empty, puffed up with deceptions. Deceived heart disposes him; they surrender to delusions of their own accord. Cannot deliver his soul: they hasten to destruction, harden hearts. Is there not a lie in my right hand: examine actions, do not flatter; try everything by the standard God laid down.

Reformed hearing: ashes are empty deceptions; the deceived heart disposes him; they surrender of their own accord; they cannot deliver the soul; ask whether the right hand holds a lie; try all by God’s standard. Shared with Wesley: feeds on ashes; deluded/deceived heart; cannot deliver; lie in the right hand. Historic idol in the right hand, not a newspaper. Quote-honesty: Calvin’s “feedeth” and “deliver his soul” are his lemmas for “feeds on ashes” and “cannot deliver himself.” Prefer no keyContrast: 20 is shared satire—the permission-versus-hardening fork stays on v. 18. Match v. 18: judicial hardening and voluntary shutting of eyes. Match v. 19: block of wood.
